title: The Story of Tea
topic: The history and trade of tea
context:
Tea is the most widely consumed beverage in the world after water, yet its origins lie in a single plant, Camellia sinensis, native to the forests of south-west China. According to legend, the emperor Shennong discovered the drink around 2737 BC when leaves from a wild tree blew into his boiling water, but archaeologists have found evidence of tea drinking only from about the second century BC. Early on, tea was valued as a medicine rather than a pleasure, and it was often boiled with onions, ginger and orange peel.

By the Tang dynasty, tea had become a fashionable drink among scholars and monks. Monks drank it to stay awake during long hours of meditation, and Buddhist travellers carried seeds to Japan in the ninth century. Tea was compressed into hard bricks for transport, and these bricks even served as currency along the trade routes of Central Asia. Under the Song dynasty, fine powdered tea was whisked in bowls, a custom that later inspired the Japanese tea ceremony.

Europeans encountered tea in the sixteenth century, when Portuguese traders brought small quantities home. It was the Dutch who first imported it on a large scale, and from there it reached Britain, where Catherine of Braganza, the wife of Charles II, helped popularise it at court. For a long time tea was so expensive that it was kept under lock and key, and smuggling flourished, since high taxes made legal tea cost far more than it should. By 1800, the British were buying so much that the East India Company needed a way to pay for it without draining its silver reserves. Meanwhile, a new social habit grew up at home: the custom of afternoon tea emerged in the 1840s, when a duchess began asking for light refreshments to fill the long gap before dinner.

The solution was a trade in opium grown in India and sold illegally in China, which led to the Opium Wars of the nineteenth century. At the same time the company sought to break China's monopoly on tea by growing the plant elsewhere. In 1848, the botanist Robert Fortune smuggled seedlings and workers out of China, and plantations were soon established in Assam and Darjeeling. Within a few decades, India and later Sri Lanka had overtaken China as major exporters.

Today the industry employs millions of workers, many of them women who pick the leaves by hand, since machines damage the delicate shoots. Wages on some plantations remain low, and campaigners have pressed companies to adopt certification schemes. Climate change is a further concern, as warmer temperatures and irregular rain are altering the flavour and yield of tea grown at high altitude. Researchers are experimenting with heat-tolerant varieties to protect the crop, although it will take years to know whether they match the taste of traditional bushes.

title: Surtsey: An Island Born from the Sea
context:
In November 1963, the crew of a fishing boat off the south coast of Iceland noticed smoke rising from the sea and the smell of sulphur. An undersea volcano was erupting, and within days a new island had appeared. Named Surtsey after the fire giant Surtr of Norse legend, it continued to grow for almost four years, until the eruptions stopped in 1967. At its largest, the island covered about 2.7 square kilometres. Its surface remained too hot to walk on for months afterwards, and steam still escaped from cracks in the cooling rock.

Almost at once, scientists recognised an extraordinary opportunity. Unlike most places on Earth, Surtsey had been born sterile, because the heat of the lava killed every living thing. Whatever arrived later would have come from elsewhere, and researchers could record the process of colonisation from the very beginning. To keep the experiment pure, the Icelandic government declared the island a protected reserve, and since then only a handful of scientists have been permitted to land there. Even they must wash their clothing and check their boots for seeds before they arrive.

The first colonists were microorganisms and simple plants. Bacteria and fungi appeared in the volcanic ash within months, and in 1965 the first flowering plant, a sea rocket, was found growing on the beach. Its seeds had been carried by ocean currents. Mosses and lichens followed, and about a decade later seagulls began nesting on the island. The birds proved decisive: their droppings fertilised the thin soil, allowing grasses and many other plants to take root where nothing could have survived before. Today more than seventy species of flowering plants have been recorded, although not all of them have lasted.

Animal life has also arrived. Insects were carried on the wind or on floating debris, and spiders sailed in on silk threads. Seals now breed on the beaches, and puffins have started to nest in burrows on the grassy slopes. Meanwhile, the island itself is shrinking. Waves and storms have eaten away the soft volcanic ash, and the surface area has halved. Geologists predict that within a few more centuries only the hard rock core will remain above the sea. Divers have also noted that kelp forests and fish have gradually established themselves around the island, completing a picture of a new ecosystem.

The scientific significance of Surtsey was recognised in 2008, when UNESCO placed it on the World Heritage List. Researchers say that the island offers lessons for conservation, because it shows how quickly ecosystems can form without human interference, and how important a single factor, such as the arrival of seabirds, can be. It also gives a preview of how life might establish itself on newly exposed land when glaciers retreat, a process that is becoming more common as the climate warms.

title: The Making of the Bicycle
context:
The bicycle in its modern form is barely a century and a half old, yet it is among the most efficient machines ever built for converting human effort into movement. Its ancestor was the running machine, or draisine, invented in 1817 by the German Baron Karl von Drais. It consisted of two wheels joined by a wooden frame, and the rider pushed along the ground with his feet. The invention was prompted by a shortage of oats after a volcanic eruption in Indonesia darkened the sky and ruined harvests, making horses expensive to feed.

The next step was the addition of pedals. In the 1860s, French makers attached cranks directly to the front wheel, producing the velocipede, nicknamed the boneshaker because its wooden wheels and iron tyres made every journey uncomfortable. To travel faster, manufacturers enlarged the front wheel, since one turn of the pedals carried the rider further. This led to the penny-farthing, with a front wheel as tall as 1.5 metres. It was fast but dangerous: a rider who struck a stone could be thrown over the handlebars, and many suffered serious injuries. Despite these flaws the machines became a craze in Paris and London, and riding schools opened to teach clumsy newcomers how to stay upright.

The breakthrough came in 1885, when the English engineer John Kemp Starley introduced the Rover safety bicycle. It had two wheels of equal size and a chain that drove the rear wheel, which meant that the rider sat low and could stop with his feet on the ground. A few years later, John Boyd Dunlop reinvented the pneumatic tyre, which was filled with air and absorbed the shocks of rough roads. Together these improvements made cycling both comfortable and safe, and sales rose dramatically.

The bicycle also had social consequences. For women in the 1890s it offered a rare chance of independent travel, and campaigners such as Susan B. Anthony declared that it had done more for female emancipation than anything else. Clothing changed, as long skirts gave way to practical divided garments known as bloomers. Cyclists' clubs organised weekend excursions, and the new mobility encouraged people to marry outside their own villages, widening the pool of partners.

In the twentieth century the arrival of the motor car reduced cycling in many wealthy countries, but it remained vital in Asia and Africa, where millions of people still depend on it for work. In recent years cities have rediscovered the bicycle as a solution to congestion and pollution. Public hire schemes allow residents to pick up a bike at one station and leave it at another, and electric models with small motors are making hilly routes accessible to riders who might once have given up. The world's bicycle fleet is now estimated at well over a billion machines.

title: The Troubles of the Honeybee
context:
Honeybees are responsible for pollinating roughly one third of the food that people eat, from almonds and apples to blueberries and coffee. In the winter of 2006, beekeepers in the United States began reporting that entire hives had been abandoned. The queen and a few young workers remained, but the thousands of adult workers had vanished, leaving no bodies behind. The phenomenon was named colony collapse disorder, and in some regions it destroyed up to ninety per cent of managed hives within weeks. Because the losses came when farmers most needed pollination, the story quickly reached newspapers and television, and governments in several countries began funding research.

Researchers quickly suspected a single cause, but the evidence pointed to several pressures acting together. One was the varroa mite, a parasite that attaches itself to bees, feeds on their fat and spreads viruses through the colony. Another was a family of pesticides called neonicotinoids, which are absorbed by plants and found in pollen and nectar. At low doses they do not kill bees outright, but experiments show that they impair navigation, so that foragers fail to find their way home to the hive.

Nutrition also matters. Large farms that grow a single crop, such as almonds, provide abundant food for a few weeks and almost none for the rest of the year. Commercial beekeepers transport hives by lorry across the country to pollinate such crops, which exposes the bees to stress and to diseases from other colonies. A diet drawn from a variety of wild flowers is more nourishing, and bees fed on a mixture of pollens show stronger immune systems than those given only one type.

Wild bees face similar threats and are often overlooked. There are more than twenty thousand species worldwide, ranging from bumblebees to tiny solitary insects that nest in holes in the ground. Many are better pollinators of particular plants than honeybees are. Bumblebees, for instance, can shake pollen loose from tomato flowers by vibrating their flight muscles at high frequency, a skill that honeybees lack. Surveys in Europe and North America have recorded sharp declines in the numbers of many wild species, largely because of the loss of meadows.

Solutions are being tested. Some countries have restricted the use of neonicotinoids on flowering crops. Farmers are encouraged to plant strips of wildflowers along field edges, and several cities have begun to leave verges uncut so that insects can feed there. Scientists are also breeding honeybees that groom themselves more thoroughly and remove mites. Yet the number of managed hives has in fact risen worldwide, which has led some critics to argue that the crisis for honeybees has been overstated and that wild species deserve more attention. Public awareness has grown too, and some gardeners now leave patches of lawn to grow wild and build simple nest boxes from hollow stems.

title: Stress and the Body
context:
Stress is often described as a feeling, but it is first of all a physical reaction. When the brain detects a threat, a small region called the hypothalamus triggers the adrenal glands, which sit on top of the kidneys, to release hormones. Adrenaline raises the heart rate and sends blood to the muscles, while cortisol increases the amount of sugar in the bloodstream. This response, known as fight or flight, evolved to help early humans escape predators, and it is useful in short bursts when a rapid reaction is needed. The body cannot tell the difference between a charging animal and an overflowing inbox, which is why modern worries can set off the same ancient alarm.

Problems arise when the response is triggered again and again. Chronic stress keeps cortisol levels high for weeks or months, and the effects spread through the body. Blood pressure remains elevated, which strains the arteries, and digestion slows down. The immune system is suppressed, so people under prolonged pressure catch colds more often. In a well-known experiment, volunteers were deliberately exposed to a cold virus, and those who reported the highest levels of stress in the preceding weeks were significantly more likely to fall ill.

Stress also affects the brain. Elevated cortisol is linked to shrinkage in the hippocampus, a region involved in memory, and students often find that they forget material they knew well when they are anxious during examinations. Sleep suffers too, creating a cycle: tired people produce more cortisol, which makes it harder to sleep. Some researchers argue that this loop helps to explain why stress and depression frequently appear together in the same patients.

Not all stress is harmful. Moderate challenges, such as preparing for a performance, can sharpen attention and improve results, a pattern psychologists describe as an inverted U: performance rises with pressure up to a peak and then falls away. Studies also suggest that attitude matters. People who are taught to see their racing heart as a sign that the body is preparing for action tend to perform better, and to show less anxiety, than those who try to suppress their nerves. Short, manageable pressure of this kind is sometimes called good stress, because it leaves people feeling energised rather than exhausted.

Coping strategies fall into several groups. Physical activity burns off stress hormones and releases endorphins, which improve mood. Relaxation techniques, such as slow breathing, activate the parasympathetic nervous system, which slows the heart. Social support is among the most powerful buffers, since people with close friends recover from stressful events more quickly. Employers are increasingly encouraged to reduce the causes of stress, for example by limiting overtime, rather than simply offering workers advice on how to be more resilient. Few of these approaches are expensive, but all of them require regular practice to be effective.

title: Living with Water in the Netherlands
context:
About a quarter of the Netherlands lies below sea level, and roughly half of the land is less than one metre above it. Without protection, much of the country would be flooded daily. For over a thousand years the Dutch have fought the water, first by building mounds called terpen to raise their homes above floods, and later by constructing dikes, the embankments that hold back the sea. Maintaining these defences has shaped the nation's politics, its economy and even its sense of identity.

A catastrophe in 1953 transformed the country's approach. A violent North Sea storm combined with high tide broke through dikes in the south-west, flooding 150,000 hectares and killing more than 1,800 people. In response, the government launched the Delta Works, a vast system of dams, sluices and storm surge barriers, completed over four decades. The most impressive element is the Oosterscheldekering, a barrier nine kilometres long whose gates close only during storms, which allows the tidal estuary behind it to keep its salt-water ecosystem. Since then the barriers have been tested several times by severe storms, and none has failed.

Land has also been created from the sea. Windmills were used from the fifteenth century to pump water out of shallow lakes into canals, producing fertile land called polders. The largest project, begun in 1920, closed off the Zuiderzee, a shallow bay, with a thirty-kilometre dam, and several sections were drained to form a new province, Flevoland. Today about one-fifth of the country's area consists of reclaimed land. Because drained peat soil shrinks and oxidises, many polders are slowly sinking, which means that the pumps must work harder every year.

Climate change has led engineers to rethink the policy of simply building higher walls. Dutch planners now speak of living with water. Under the Room for the River programme, completed in 2015, dikes were moved back, floodplains were lowered and secondary channels were dug at more than thirty locations, giving rivers space to rise safely. In cities, car parks and public squares are being designed to fill with rainwater temporarily during heavy storms, a technique that relieves pressure on the drains. Residents are asked to accept that occasional flooding of designated areas is a fair price for greater safety elsewhere.

Dutch expertise is now an export. Engineering firms advise cities from Jakarta to New Orleans on managing flood risk, and Dutch universities train foreign specialists. Critics point out, however, that the country's success rests on money and strong institutions, namely the regional water boards, which have collected taxes and managed defences for centuries and are among the oldest democratic bodies in Europe. Copying the technology without the governance, they argue, will not work. The model also depends on public willingness to pay for protection that may rarely be needed.

title: Why Did the Classic Maya Cities Fall?
context:
The Classic Maya civilisation, centred in the lowlands of present-day Mexico, Guatemala and Belize, reached its height between about AD 250 and 900. Its cities, such as Tikal and Calakmul, contained pyramids, palaces and ball courts, and supported populations of tens of thousands of people. The Maya developed a sophisticated writing system, an accurate calendar and advanced mathematics, including the concept of zero, centuries before it was widely used in Europe. Their astronomers tracked the movements of Venus with remarkable precision, and priests used this knowledge to guide religious ceremonies and the timing of wars.

Between about 800 and 950, however, many of the great southern cities were abandoned. Building ceased, monuments stopped carrying dated inscriptions, and the population fell sharply. The collapse has fascinated scholars for more than a century, and early theories blamed a single cause, such as invasion or disease. Today most researchers argue that several pressures combined. Intensive farming had stripped forests from the hills, causing soil erosion, while a growing population placed heavy demands on a fragile environment that had little room for error.

Drought appears to have played a central role. Scientists have analysed sediment from Lake Chichancanab and mineral deposits in caves, which record rainfall over thousands of years. The evidence shows a series of severe dry spells during the ninth and tenth centuries, some lasting a decade. Because the Maya relied on rainfall and stored water in reservoirs rather than using large rivers, they were especially vulnerable. When harvests failed repeatedly, rulers lost their authority, since their claim to power rested on the ability to bring rain through ritual. Later droughts, including one in the sixteenth century, show that the regional climate has long been unpredictable, and farmers there still plan their planting around the arrival of the rains.

Warfare added to the strain. Inscriptions record growing conflict between rival city-states, and archaeologists have found fortifications built in haste around some centres. Trade routes were disrupted, which prevented cities from importing food when local crops failed. People did not vanish overnight; instead they moved gradually to the north of the Yucatán peninsula and to the coast, where cities such as Chichen Itza flourished for another two centuries before declining in their turn. Some scholars point out that northern settlements had access to underground water sources called cenotes, which gave them an advantage during dry years.

The Maya did not disappear. About six million people in Mexico and Central America still speak Mayan languages today, and many follow traditions that date back to their ancestors. Archaeologists have also learned that earlier estimates of the ancient population were too low, since airborne laser scanning has revealed thousands of previously unknown structures hidden beneath the forest canopy, including roads, farms and fortifications. These discoveries suggest that the Maya landscape was far more densely settled than anyone had realised.

title: The Psychology of Colour
context:
Colour influences how we feel more than most of us realise, yet scientists caution that the effects are smaller and more complicated than popular books claim. The perception of colour begins in the retina, where three types of cone cells respond to red, green and blue light. The brain combines their signals to create the full range of shades that we see. About one in twelve men has a form of colour blindness, usually involving difficulty in distinguishing red from green, compared with roughly one in two hundred women. Colour vision is also not perfectly stable: the same shirt can look blue in daylight and purple under a lamp, because the brain adjusts for the light around it.

Many studies have examined the link between colour and emotion. Red is associated in several cultures with danger and excitement, and one well-known study found that athletes wearing red in combat sports won slightly more often than those wearing blue. Critics note that the effect is small and may depend on the sport, the referees and the audience. Blue, in contrast, is often described as calming, and it is the most frequently chosen favourite colour in surveys carried out across many different countries.

Cultural differences matter greatly. White is the colour of weddings in much of Europe, but in parts of East Asia it is traditionally worn at funerals. Green signifies luck in Ireland, while in some other places it is linked to illness or envy. Language may shape perception as well. Russian has separate basic words for light blue and dark blue, and Russian speakers have been shown to distinguish between the two shades slightly faster than English speakers, who use a single word for both.

Businesses make use of colour constantly. Fast food chains often use red and yellow, which are thought to stimulate appetite and create a sense of urgency, while banks favour blue to convey stability and trust. Evidence for such effects is limited, though. Brand colours seem to work chiefly by making a company recognisable, and consistency matters more than any particular shade. In hospitals, designers choose soft greens and blues to reduce anxiety, although the benefits are hard to separate from other aspects of the environment such as noise and lighting.

Colour may also affect performance. Some experiments suggest that exposure to red before a test can reduce results, perhaps because the colour is linked with failure through teachers' red pens. Other studies find that a view of green nature improves concentration and creativity. Replication has proved difficult for many colour studies, and researchers now emphasise larger samples and more careful controls. The emerging consensus is that colour acts as a subtle cue rather than a powerful force, and that context decides its meaning. This does not make colour unimportant to designers; it means that its effects are usually modest and easily overwhelmed by shape, texture and meaning.

title: Farming Upwards
context:
By 2050 the world's population is expected to reach nearly ten billion, and feeding everyone will require much more food from limited land. One response is vertical farming, in which crops are grown in stacked layers inside buildings, often without soil. Plants sit in trays or on towers, their roots bathed in water containing dissolved nutrients, a method known as hydroponics. Some systems use a fine mist instead, called aeroponics, which uses even less water and can allow roots to absorb oxygen more effectively than a flooded tray.

The advantages are considerable. Because the environment is controlled, crops can be grown all year, whatever the weather outside. Vertical farms use up to ninety per cent less water than conventional fields, since the water circulates and is recycled. They need no pesticides, as insects cannot enter sealed rooms, and they can be built in or near cities, which cuts the distance that produce must travel. Leafy vegetables and herbs, which are delicate and spoil quickly, benefit most from being grown close to the people who eat them. Growers also report that harvests are predictable, so supermarkets can plan their orders weeks ahead and waste is reduced.

Light is the central challenge. Plants need specific wavelengths for photosynthesis, and farms replace sunshine with LED lamps tuned to the red and blue colours that leaves absorb best. Engineers can adjust the spectrum to change the taste, size or colour of a crop. However, the lamps consume large amounts of electricity, which accounts for as much as a quarter or more of operating costs. If the power comes from fossil fuels, much of the environmental benefit disappears, so some farms are being built next to wind or solar installations.

Economic performance has been mixed. Several high-profile companies have struggled, because buildings, equipment and energy are expensive while vegetable prices are low. A kilo of lettuce from a vertical farm usually costs more than one grown outdoors. Staple crops like wheat and rice, which supply most of the world's calories, are far too cheap and need too much space and light to be grown this way. Critics conclude that vertical farms will remain a niche supplier of premium produce for wealthy city dwellers. Several large operators have already closed sites after rising electricity prices wiped out their margins.

Supporters respond that the technology is improving. Robots now plant, move and harvest trays, reducing labour, and sensors monitor plants individually so that growers can respond to problems within hours. Strawberries and tomatoes, once thought impractical, are being grown commercially in several countries. In places with little arable land or harsh climates, such as deserts and polar regions, vertical farms may offer fresh food where almost none was possible before, which could make them valuable even if they never feed the whole world. Some industry leaders now admit that their early promises were too ambitious.

title: The Whistling Language of La Gomera
context:
On La Gomera, one of the Canary Islands, shepherds and farmers have for centuries communicated across deep ravines by whistling. The whistled speech, called Silbo Gomero, can carry a message up to five kilometres across the steep valleys, far beyond the range of a shout. It is not a code but a way of speaking Spanish: whistlers reproduce the sounds of the language in two or four pitches, which listeners decode as words. A skilled whistler can send a complete sentence, from a greeting to a warning about a stray animal, in a few seconds.

Whistled languages exist in more than seventy communities around the world, from the mountains of northern Turkey to villages in Mexico and the rainforests of the Amazon. They tend to arise in places where the terrain makes ordinary speech difficult, such as mountains, dense forest or islands with scattered homes. Because whistling is louder and travels farther than the voice, it allows people to talk across distances while they work in the fields, and it requires no equipment. Whistled speech is usually learned in childhood, alongside the ordinary spoken language, rather than as a separate skill taught later.

Scientists have studied the brain to understand how whistled speech is processed. Normally, language is handled mainly by the left hemisphere, while melodies and pitch are processed by the right. Research on whistlers in Turkey found that listeners to whistled words used both hemispheres, which suggests that the brain adapts to the type of signal it receives. In the case of Silbo, experienced whistlers can distinguish whistled vowels and consonants, showing that the process is truly linguistic rather than musical. The findings have helped neuroscientists to question the older view that language is processed in one fixed place.

Despite its beauty, the tradition came close to disappearing. As roads were built and mobile phones arrived, fewer people had any need for long-distance whistling, and by the 1970s only a small number of elderly islanders could still use it. Worried by the decline, the island's government introduced Silbo into schools in 1999, and today all children on La Gomera learn it as part of the curriculum. In 2009, UNESCO recognised the whistled language as part of the world's intangible cultural heritage. Tourism has helped by creating demand for demonstrations, and local restaurants now display signs about the language.

Revival has not been without controversy. Some older whistlers argue that classroom learning cannot replace the experience of using the language in real situations, and that children may come to treat it as a performance for tourists. Others reply that preserving the skill in any form is better than losing it altogether. Whatever the verdict, the story of Silbo has encouraged communities elsewhere to record their own whistled languages before the last fluent speakers are gone.
